Becca Thomases
Professor of Mathematical Sciences
Smith College


I study the mathematics of fluid motion, with an emphasis on complex fluids, computational modeling, and nonlinear dynamics.
My research combines mathematical analysis and numerical simulation to explore how fluids flow, deform, and organize.
Explore my research

title: Mentoring & Teaching
text:
One of the things I enjoy most about being at Smith College is working with undergraduate students on mathematical questions. I particularly enjoy helping students make the transition from learning established mathematical methods to using those methods to investigate questions whose answers are not yet known.
My research projects often involve mathematical modeling, numerical simulation, and scientific computing. Students bring different backgrounds and levels of experience, and learning new tools together is frequently part of the process.

title: Mentoring & Teaching
text:
Undergraduate Research
There are several ways for Smith students to become involved in mathematical research.
MTH 301 — Research in Mathematics
MTH 301 provides opportunities to participate in faculty-supervised research projects during the academic year. Students work individually or in small groups, exploring mathematical questions and developing their approaches over the semester.
Summer research
Summer research provides an opportunity for sustained work on a mathematical problem, often in collaboration with other students and faculty. Projects may involve theoretical analysis, developing computational models, running simulations, or interpreting numerical results.
Independent study and special studies
For students with a particular mathematical interest, an independent study can provide a more individualized opportunity to explore a subject or research question in depth. The scope and preparation depend on the project.
Students don’t need to arrive with a fully formed research question; exploring possible questions is part of the process.
Smith students interested in mathematical research are welcome to contact me at bthomases@smith.edu. My availability to supervise research projects varies throughout the academic year and from summer to summer.

title: Mentoring & Teaching
text:
Teaching
I teach courses across the mathematics curriculum, including calculus, linear algebra, and applied mathematics. I especially enjoy helping students develop mathematical intuition through experimentation, computation, and discussion.
One example is MTH 261: Computational Linear Algebra, a course I developed and first taught in Spring 2025. Students use MATLAB extensively to explore mathematical ideas through computational experiments, emphasizing the interplay between mathematical reasoning, numerical methods, and hands-on investigation.

title: Mentoring & Teaching
text:
CAMP
I also created MTH 263: Computational and Applied Mathematics Practicum (CAMP), an intensive January-term course introducing students to computational research through open-ended projects, collaborative exploration, and opportunities to communicate results. Its first offering as a Smith course is scheduled for Interterm 2027.
Learn more about CAMP

title: CAMP
text:
CAMP is an intensive introduction to research in computational and applied mathematics at Smith College. The program gives undergraduate students an opportunity to explore mathematical research, develop computational skills, and experience what it means to work on an open-ended problem.
No prior research experience is required. Students learn by doing: experimenting with computational methods, developing questions, discussing ideas, and communicating their progress.

title: CAMP
text:
Learning how to do research
CAMP combines short lessons in computational mathematics with substantial time for independent exploration. Students learn to use tools such as MATLAB while developing the less formal skills that research requires: formulating questions, troubleshooting, documenting progress, working collaboratively, and communicating results.
Rather than aiming for a polished research result in two weeks, the program emphasizes learning how to begin and sustain a research investigation.





Presentations, collaborative computing, and hands-on exploration during CAMP 2026.

title: CAMP
section: From pilot program to Smith course
text:
From pilot program to Smith course
CAMP began as a pilot program in May 2025 with five students. A second offering in January 2026 expanded to fifteen students.
Building on these experiences, CAMP has been approved as MTH 263, a two-credit Smith College January-term course, beginning in January 2027.
The course offers students a structured but exploratory introduction to computational research, with opportunities to pursue questions suited to their interests and preparation.
The CAMP pilots and the development of the teaching resources were supported by the Richard Lounsbery Foundation.


The inaugural CAMP cohort, May 2025.

title: CAMP
text:
Resources for instructors
CAMP was designed to be adaptable. Instructors interested in offering a similar program can use the practical replication guide and companion teaching materials.
The materials include sample schedules and syllabi, MATLAB activities, project-scoping exercises, student reflection templates, presentation prompts, and assessment resources.


Practical Replication Guide
A short guide to organizing a CAMP-style program, including its structure, daily routines, and practical advice.
Download the replication guide (PDF)


Teaching Resource Package
Editable teaching materials, computational exercises, templates, and sample datasets.

These materials are provided for adaptation to other instructional settings. Some were used during the 2025–2026 pilots; others were developed for subsequent offerings.

title: Research
text:
My research lies at the intersection of applied mathematics, fluid mechanics, and scientific computing. I use mathematical models, numerical simulation, and collaborations with experimentalists to investigate how fluids behave when their dynamics are shaped by elasticity, complex microstructure, and interactions with moving bodies.
A recurring theme is the emergence of unexpected dynamics from relatively simple mathematical models: instabilities, coherent structures, periodic motion, and transitions to irregular behavior.

title: Research
text:
Complex fluids and nonlinear dynamics


Even in the absence of inertia, viscoelastic fluids can exhibit remarkably complicated dynamics. Elastic stresses interact with fluid motion, producing instabilities, coherent structures, and sustained time-dependent flow.
I study these phenomena using numerical simulations and mathematical models, including the Oldroyd-B equations. Recent work explores periodic and more complicated dynamics in model flows, including Kolmogorov flow and the four-roll mill.
A central question is how relatively simple constitutive models give rise to complex spatiotemporal behavior.



Structures in a viscoelastic flow simulation.

title: Research
text:
Elastoviscoplastic fluids


Many materials combine elastic deformation, viscous flow, and yielding. Examples include gels, pastes, and suspensions, which can behave like solids under some conditions and flow like liquids under others.
My research examines how plasticity changes the dynamics of viscoelastic flows, using mathematical models such as the Saramito elastoviscoplastic model.
An especially interesting question is how yielding can both suppress and reorganize flow instabilities, leading to nontrivial transitions between distinct dynamical regimes.



Flow structures in elastoviscoplastic models.

title: Research
text:
Swimming and fluid–structure interactions


How does the rheology of a surrounding fluid influence the motion of a swimmer?
I study the interaction between deforming bodies and complex fluids, including sperm swimming in Newtonian and viscoelastic environments. This work connects mathematical modeling and computation with experimental observations of swimming kinematics.
These problems reveal how the interplay between fluid stresses, flexible structures, and prescribed or internally generated motion influences locomotion.



Experimental sperm flagellar shapes and reconstructed centerlines.

title: Research
section: Learning to swim: reinforcement learning and cilia
text:
Learning to swim: reinforcement learning and cilia


A newer direction in my research uses reinforcement learning to explore locomotion strategies in viscous fluids.
Beginning with simple bead-based models of cilia, we compare learned strokes with computationally determined optimal solutions. These small systems provide useful benchmarks for understanding how learning algorithms discover effective periodic motion.
The longer-term goal is to extend these ideas to more flexible swimmers and investigate how geometry, hydrodynamic interactions, and fluid rheology shape optimal locomotion.



Reconstructed strokes from a computational cilium model.
